## Nonlinear Performance Degradation Prediction of Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells Using Relevance Vector Machine

Yiming Wu , Student Member, IEEE , Elena Breaz , Member, IEEE , Fei Gao , Senior Member, IEEE , Damien Paire, and Abdellatif Miraoui , Senior Member, IEEE

Abstract -Environmental issues, especially global warming due to the greenhouse effect, have become more and more critical in recent decades. As one potential candidate among different alternative 'green energy' solutions for sustainable development, the proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) has received extensive research attention for many years for energy and transportation applications. However, the relatively short lifespan of PEMFCs operating under non-steady-state conditions (for vehicles, for example) impedes its massive use. The accurate prediction of their aging mechanisms can thus help to design proper maintenance patterns of PEMFCs by providing foreseeable performance degradation information. In addition, the prediction could also help to avoid or mitigate the unwanted degradation of PEMFC systems during operation. In this paper, an advanced self-adaptive relevance vector machine (RVM) has been developed and demonstrated to predict the performance degradation of PEMFCs. In order to prove the versatility of proposed RVM method, the predictive results are experimentally validated using two different PEMFC stacks aging data under different operating patterns. Furthermore, the obtained results are compared with results from both classic support vector machine and original RVM methods in order to highlight the effectiveness of the proposed self-adaptive RVM method with a modified design matrix. A comparison between single-step-ahead and multiple-step-ahead predictions of the proposed method is also given and discussed. The results show that the proposed novel RVM method is powerful and effective for PEMFC degradation prediction.

Index Terms -Aging prediction, long-term degradation, proton exchange membrane fuel cell, relevance vector machine.

## I. INTRODUCTION

T HE proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFC), also abbreviated as the PEMFCs, can produce electricity directly from electrochemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen in the air, with the only by-products of water and heat. If the hydrogen is produced from renewable energy sources, this energy conversion is 100% eco-friendly. The PEMFCs are

getting more and more attention because they are considered as potential candidates of clean energy solution in the near future. Besides, the PEMFCs contain no moving parts in the structures, this feature ensures both compactness and reliability of fuel cell systems. Thus, the PEMFCs are especially considered to be used in transportation applications such as hybrid or electrical vehicles.

The performance of PEMFCs is strongly influenced by the operating conditions, which may cause performance degradation [1]. However, the structural and physical complexity of PEMFCs still make the accurate prediction of fuel cell performance degradation a great challenge today. In general, the aging prediction can be separated to model-based [2], [3], data-driven [4]-[6] and hybrid prediction approaches [7], [8]. Generally speaking, the model-based method provides prediction or performance evaluation based on the specific physical model of one component or the whole of a PEMFC stack. The data-driven approach stands for the methodologies evaluating the performance degradation by analyzing the variation of the degradation data with machine learning or data mining based solutions. The hybrid prediction approach is achieved by combining physical and mathematical model into PEMFC degradation evaluation. From a practical point of view, the data driven approaches show more interests compared with the other two, because they are easy to deploy, less computationally expensive and more flexible to represent non-linear features observed in the aging data. However, it should be noted that, the observed non-linear fuel cell performance degradation curve is caused by multiple complex electrochemical phenomena during fuel cell operation and is highly dependent on operation conditions. Thus, it is difficult to find a simple pattern to represent and predict the observed non-linearity. This feature more or less limits the effectiveness of classic mathematical regression solutions such as linear least square regression.

Consequently, the non-linear regression methods are thought to have potential to cope with the fuel cell non-linear aging prediction problem. Although the non-linear regression methods have been used in the literature for Lithium-ion battery performance degradation modeling and prediction [9]-[11], there are only few papers in the literature [4]-[6] which discussed fuel cell aging/degradation modeling and prediction using nonlinear regression approaches. Recently, relevance vector machines (RVM) are getting more and more attention in the field of classification and regression analysis. The RVM approach uses Bayesian based filtering framework that could provide at the same time the predictive results and the corresponding confidence intervals. This feature is particularly useful when dealing with non-linear and uncertain prediction problems [12]. The RVM was firstly introduced by Tipping [12]-[15] around 2001, and has the identical functional form with the support vector machine (SVM). It should be noted that, RVM and SVM are both kernel function based methods and are both efficient when coping with non-linear regression and prediction problems. However, the RVM shows more advantages than classic SVM in the case of predictive problems with uncertainties, because RVM usually requires less training sets and it can present probabilistic results.

Even though the RVM is a relatively new mathematical tool, there are already some papers regarding the applications of RVM in various research fields. For example, Zio and Maio [16] mathematically used the RVM approach to estimate and predict the fatigue or degradation data described by Paris-Erdogan model. They also made a comparison of the results with particle filter and fuzzy similarity-based approach, and RVM shows clearly better prediction performance in terms of data requirements, accuracy and computational demand. Moreover, the state of health (SOH) of Li-ion battery was successfully predicted using RVM by Li et al. in [17]. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of RVM when applying to online battery prognostics. Barr´ e et al. [18] proposed also a real-time method based on RVM to predict the SOH and remaining useful life (RUL) of lithium-ion battery in electric vehicles. Another prognostic work of Li-ion battery is proposed by Wang et al. in [19]. In their paper, the prediction is achieved by creating a three-parameter battery capacity degradation model with the relevance vectors after training the original data set by RVM. The results showed relatively good performance of RVM in practical cases.

This paper is a major extension of our previous works demonstrated in [20], [21], with significant improvements on kernel width selection and non-linear prediction accuracy of the PEMFC performance degradation. In this paper, a novel approach for the predictions of voltage degradation of two different types of PEMFCs (NEXA stack and PM 200 stack) based on the implementations of RVM is developed and discussed. This work is structured as follows: Section II shows firstly a brief background of PEMFC working principles and main aging and degradation factors during its operation. Section III presents the mathematical formulation of RVM. Section IV then focuses on the implementation of RVM with different data sets for the prediction of PEMFC voltage degradation curve. In section V, the obtained regression and prediction results of modified RVM are illustrated, then followed by the detailed performance evaluation and comparison with both classic SVM and original RVM in Section VI. Furthermore, comparisons between several multistep-ahead predictions are demonstrated in Section VII. Finally in Section VIII, the conclusions are given.

## II. AGING FACTORS DURING PEMFC OPERATION

APEMFCis an electrochemical energy converter, which can directly generate electricity from the electrochemical reaction between oxygen (from air) and hydrogen gas.

Fig. 1 shows a typical layout of PEMFC [22], [23]. During its operation, the hydrogen is supplied to the anode side and the oxygen is supplied to the cathode side. The hydrogen and oxygen are then diffused through the gas diffusion layer (GDL) to the catalyst layer on each side. At anode catalyst layer, the hydrogen molecules are disassociated to protons and electrons. The protons then migrate through the humidified polymer electrolyte (membrane) from the anode side to the cathode side, while at the same time the electrons are conducted through the external circuit from anode to cathode to form the electrical current. Finally, at the cathode catalyst layer, the protons, the electrons and the oxygen molecules are combined to form water as byproduct. However, the electrochemical reactions in the PEMFCs are not perfect, different kinds of degradation would happen during fuel cell operation [24]. Generally, most of the degradations take place in GDL, catalyst layer and polymer membrane. In the GDL, the major degradation phenomenon is carbon corrosion. The GDL is usually made of carbon paper or cloth. In most cases the carbon corrosion is the result of high humidity and/or potential (load) cycling of the PEMFC [25]-[27]. Furthermore, the platinum (catalyst) dissolution or reorganization (sintering) in the catalyst layer are also commonly considered as critical factors influencing long-term performance of PEMFC. The platinum particles are attached on the surface of carbon support in electrodes, so it is vulnerable when carbon structure starts to degrade. Besides, the platinum particles sintering can be commonly observed under load cycling and/or operating conditions such as high humidity or high temperature [28]- [30]. For the polymer membrane, it is believed that the chemical attacks caused by hydroxyl (OH · ) and peroxyl (OOH · ) radicals initiate the membrane degradation. By applying the above-proposed RVM method, five data sets from two different types of fuel cells are tested.

Case study 1 : 1.2 kW Ballard NEXA commercial fuel cell stack (47 cells) working under four different operation conditions. (4 data sets)

Case study 2 : 8 kW PM 200 PEMFC stack (96 cells) working under mobile/dynamic application. (1 data set)

All of the five data sets are the experimentally measured fuel cell stack output voltage values during about 400 to 450 hours of continuous fuel cell operation, and each of them contains around 100 data points. Specifically, the 4 data sets of the 1.2 kW Ballard NEXA stack were measured and post-processed under steady-state operation conditions of 12 A 30 ° C, 30 A 35 ° C, 36 A 40 ° C and 44 A 40 ° C respectively. The data set of the PM 200 stack was measured under cyclic load condition with a current density profile varies between 0.30-0.97 A/ cm 2 , and two start/stops per operation hour. The detailed operation conditions and the V-I characteristics (polarization curves) of NEXA and PM 200 fuel cell stacks are listed in Table II and illustrated in Fig. 3 respectively.

For a given fuel cell stack and operation conditions, we have N data points in one data set, which can be expressed in the form of ( x 1 , t 1 ) , ( x 2 , t 2 ) , . . . , ( xi, t i ) , . . . , ( xN , tN ) . xi represents the sampling time and ti represents the corresponding stack output voltage measured at time xi . The index N denotes the total number of data points in each data set.

In this paper, we propose a novel dynamically updated training algorithm using RVM method. With s initial training points ( x 1 , t 1 ) , ( x 2 , t 2 ) , . . . , ( xs, ts ) , the RVM model is trained first to calculate the corresponding weight vector w s . Then the values of the new voltage ˜ ys +1 at new time point xs +1 can be predicted from the trained model. When the system reaches time xs +1 , the newly measured voltage ts +1 is added into the updated data set ( x 1 , t 1 ) , ( x 2 , t 2 ) , . . . , ( xs +1 , t s +1) , and the RVM model is trained again to get the new weight vector w s +1 to predict ˜ ys +2 at time point xs +2 . The same sequence is repeated for ˜ ys +3 , ˜ ys +4 . . . etc. That is to say, for N training points, we need to train and predict iteratively for ( N - s ) times (i.e., ( N - s ) times one-step-ahead predictions) to get the prediction result [˜ ys +1 , ˜ ys +2 , . . . , ˜ yN ] . This iterative dynamic training method can ensure a higher prediction accuracy. It has also to be noted that, even the RVM model need to be re-trained at each time point in our proposed algorithm, the training time with a given data set is relatively short (less than 1 s in our cases with up to 100 data points). Thus, it can be seen as a real time prediction method. The proposed RVM training steps are developed in detail hereafter:

Step 3: Adaptive kernel of δ

The Gaussian kernel function in the design matrix Φ ( x ) is expressed as k ( xi, xn ) = exp( - || xi - xn || 2 2 δ 2 ) . The δ , which is called the kernel width, plays an important role in linear or non-linear regression of RVM method and its value should be carefully tuned. If it is overestimated, the exponential will behave almost linearly and the higher-dimensional projection will start to lose its non-linear feature. On the other hand, if it is underestimated, the predictive curve would be highly sensitive to noise in the training data which could lead to the over fitting problem [20]. ## V. RESULTS AND ANALYSIS

In order to verify experimentally the effectiveness and the validity of the proposed modified RVM approach, the method is applied to each test case. It has to be noted that, the results presented in this section correspond to single-step-ahead prediction results from the proposed modified RVM (i.e. the corresponding prediction time is about 4 hours). Multi-step-ahead prediction (up to 20 hours) will be discussed later in Section VII.

## A. Case Study 1

In this first case, four experimental output voltage degradation data sets of a 1.2 kW PEMFC stack (Ballard NEXA commercial fuel cell stack) for 400 h operation under different working conditions are presented. The data sets are used to train the modified RVM model, and the predicted results are then compared with the measured ones in order to validate experimentally the prediction method proposed in this paper. For each of the data sets, we impose in this study the initial number of data points s = 15 , which indicates the first 15 data points are selected to initiate the prediction. By applying the previously developed RVM method, the model predicted results are shown and discussed hereafter.

## VIII. CONCLUSION

In this paper, an improved method of RVM has been proposed for the use of PEMFC performance degradation prognosis. At the beginning, the structure of a single cell and how it works during operation to generate electricity have been briefly descripted, followed with a summary of main factors influencing the lifespan of PEMFC. Then the proposed nonlinear mathematical approach of RVM has been developed and illustrated thoroughly, followed by a detailed description of algorithm implementation process. Compared with conventional RVMformulation, two enhancements of RVM are proposed and complied:

- 1) Comparing with the all kernel function based design matrix in conventional RVM approach, the design matrix proposed in this paper was extended by appending with non-kernel columns in order to acquire both linear and non-linear features from the fuel cell degradation data during training;
- 2) An innovative adaptive kernel width determination algorithm, which can iteratively choose the most effective kernel width value from different training data set, has been proposed in order to make training or learning process more intelligent and effective.

The advanced self-adaptive approach of RVM is then trained and implemented using experimental voltage degradation data from two different PEMFC stacks (1.2 kW and 8 kW). The predicted results of this improved RVM method show a great agreement with the experimental results under different operation conditions. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, the error assessments of prediction results have also been compared with that of classic SVM method. The results analysis convincingly showed that, the proposed modified RVM could achieve better performance than classic SVM approach. In general cases, the errors of RVM are 30%- 40% less than that of classic SVM, specifically in terms of the MAPE and RMSE. Moreover, the prediction results from the proposed modified RVM method are also compared with the results from original RVM. The comparison results indicated clearly that, the proposed modified RVM could achieve higher accuracy and shows higher potential to follow observed nonlinearity. Furthermore, comparisons and discussion between single-step-ahead and multi-step-ahead prediction from the proposedmodifiedRVMarealsoprovided.Theresultsshowthatthe modified RVM can still achieve acceptable prediction accuracy in multi-step-ahead prediction, which could provide up to 20 hours forecast time for proper maintenance planning of the studied fuel cells.

In conclusion, this advanced self-adaptive approach of RVM was demonstrated to have good accuracy and effectiveness in the context of prognostics and health management of PEMFC systems.
